title: NestJS
summary: Modules, dependency injection and the request lifecycle.
why: Nest generates a lot of structure fast. Understanding DI, modules and the request lifecycle tells you why something runs, or does not, instead of copy-pasting until it works.

cards.question: What are modules, controllers and providers in Nest?
cards.answer: Modules group related functionality. Controllers receive requests and delegate. Providers (services, repositories) hold the logic and can be injected into other classes.

cards.question: How does dependency injection work in Nest and what is its benefit?
cards.answer: The container reads constructor dependencies and resolves them by token. Providers are singletons by default, with optional request or transient scope. It makes swapping them for test doubles easy.

cards.question: In what order does the request lifecycle run?
cards.answer: Middleware, guards, interceptors (before), pipes, controller handler, interceptors (after) and, on error, exception filters.

cards.question: Guard or middleware for authorization?
cards.answer: A guard knows the execution context (which handler and metadata will run) and decides with canActivate, so it fits roles and permissions. Middleware is generic, Express-style, and does not know which handler comes next.

cards.question: How do you validate input with DTOs?
cards.answer: With ValidationPipe and classes decorated with class-validator. Enable whitelist (strips undeclared properties, preventing mass assignment) and transform to get typed instances.

cards.question: What are custom providers and when do you use them?
cards.answer: They control how a dependency is created: useClass, useValue and useFactory (which can be async and inject other providers). Used for configuration, external clients, or binding implementations to abstraction tokens.

cards.question: What do you do about a circular dependency between modules or services?
cards.answer: forwardRef() solves it technically, but it usually signals a design problem. Better to extract the shared part into a third module or service, or communicate through events to break the cycle.
